items.title: 5.9.1 Factors affecting the boiling points of liquids

source_refs.note: Topic 5.9.1, printed pages 107-108 (Table 5.4), with Quick Check 5.7 as the self-check.

blocks.text: The stronger the intermolecular forces, the lower the vapour pressure and the higher the boiling point. The higher boiling point of water shows stronger intermolecular forces than those of ethanol and methanol.

blocks.caption: Boiling points of some common liquids at 760 torr (Table 5.4)

blocks.text: Since a liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure, changing the external pressure changes the boiling point. At high external pressure the liquid needs more heat to raise its vapour pressure to the external pressure, so the boiling point rises; at lower external pressure it absorbs less heat and boils at a lower temperature. Water boils at 120 degrees C at 1489 torr and at 25 degrees C at 23.7 torr; it boils at 98 degrees C in the Murree hills, where the external pressure is 700 torr, and at only 69 degrees C at the top of Mount Everest at 323 torr. A pressure cooker raises the external pressure artificially: it is a closed container in which the water vapour cannot escape, so it builds up more pressure on the water surface and the boiling temperature rises; more heat is absorbed by the water and food cooks quickly.
